summary.one_line: A Kolkata-based, tender-driven IT/network system integrator whose reported profits have jumped, but cash has not come in. Operating cash flow was negative in FY26, receivables run at 280 days, and the entire fresh issue goes to fund more working capital. Reported growth, no moat, weak cash conversion and a thin governance record: avoid.
bull_points: Restated revenue from operations grew from ₹34.10 cr (FY24) to ₹60.53 cr (FY26), a 33.24% CAGR, and restated PAT rose from ₹1.48 cr to ₹10.22 cr (S1, S2)

Reported EBITDA margin expanded from 6.56% (FY24) to 21.97% (FY26). The company's own 'operating EBITDA', which strips out other income and adds back write-offs, still improved from 15.04% to 19.34% (S1)
Balance sheet debt is low: debt-to-equity was 0.10 at FY26, with total borrowings of about ₹2.71 cr (S1, S2)
There is a small recurring base: fibre-infrastructure leasing (₹7.22 cr, 11.93% of FY26 revenue) under a DoT IP-I registration, plus AMC/facility services (₹2.24 cr, 3.69%) (S1)
Customer dependence on the single largest client fell sharply, from 60.93% of revenue in FY25 to 25.21% in FY26, as non-government revenue rose to 26.90% (S1)
bear_points: Profit is not turning into cash. Operating cash flow was -₹6.77 cr in FY26 against PAT of ₹10.22 cr. Cumulative FY24-26 operating cash flow was ₹4.64 cr against cumulative PAT of ₹17.53 cr (S1)
Trade receivables were ₹54.98 cr at FY26, equal to 90.83% of revenue (280 days). ₹10.17 cr of this is over one year old, which is 38.31% of net worth (S1)
FY26 profit was helped by ₹2.93 cr of old creditor balances written back as income, about 21.5% of pre-tax profit (S1)

Restatement cut audited PAT: FY26 audited ₹11.73 cr became ₹10.22 cr restated, and FY24 ₹2.04 cr became ₹1.48 cr. Separately, the RHP lists historical ROC filing errors, charges that were never registered, and delayed TDS/ESIC/EPF filings (S1)

Concentration is extreme: the top 10 customers were 94.19% of FY26 revenue and three states (Bihar, Odisha, West Bengal) were 80.04%. The tender win rate fell from 41.07% to 30.43% over three years (S1)
Of the ₹42.44 cr issue, ₹5.04 cr is an OFS by the promoter. Of the fresh money, up to ₹30 cr just funds receivables and working capital, not capacity or technology (S1, S2)
watch_points: Final subscription on 29 Sep 2026, especially whether the QIB (ex-anchor) book fills. It was at 0.00x at the end of day 1 (S7, S12)
Whether FY27 half-year results show receivables being collected and operating cash flow turning positive (S1)
Outcome of the Companies Act compounding application filed on 31 Jul 2026 for the incorrect AOC-4 filings (S1)
Grey market premium readings conflict, ranging from ₹0 to ₹16 across trackers. It is unofficial and not a basis for the decision (S4, S5, S9)

reasoning: The use of proceeds tells the story. Up to ₹30 cr of the fresh issue goes to working capital in FY27-28 (₹10 cr and ₹20 cr), because management projects receivables rising from ₹54.98 cr to ₹94.52 cr and plans to pay suppliers faster, lengthening the cash conversion cycle from 14 to 103 days. IPO money is being used to fund slow-paying customers, not to build an asset or a capability (S1)

The earnings are lower quality than the headline growth suggests. FY26 operating cash flow was -₹6.77 cr on ₹10.22 cr PAT. About 21.5% of pre-tax profit came from writing back old creditor balances. Receivables over a year old reached 38.31% of net worth, and the restated PAT was cut by about ₹1.5 cr from the audited figure (S1)

There is no identifiable moat. This is a tender-based system integrator that resells OEM hardware (switches, CCTV, AV, racks) and wins mostly on lowest bid. Listed peers such as Dynacons have over 20 times the income. The win rate has fallen from 41.07% to 30.43%, and the RHP makes no import-substitution, technology or market-share claim (S1)

Revenue visibility is thin and concentrated. The top 10 customers are 94.19% of revenue, three eastern states are 80.04%, and the number of successful tenders fell from 23 to 14. Tenders won in FY26 totalled only ₹10.40 cr by bid value against ₹60.53 cr of revenue, and the RHP does not explain the gap (S1)

Governance is still being built. Independent directors and the audit committee date from June-July 2026. The RHP discloses incorrect statutory filings, unregistered charges, MSME payment delays (₹3.88 cr disallowed under Section 43B(h)) and restatement adjustments. Related-party sales to promoter-group entities in the same line of business, plus a promoter-linked company that is larger than BMISL itself, add conflict risk (S1)

Promoter quality is not in doubt on integrity: there is no litigation against them, and the promoter group keeps 72.97% post-issue with a 3-year lock on 20%. But the SME structure (1-year lock on the rest, a ₹2.64 lakh minimum ticket, no monitoring agency because the issue is under ₹50 cr) gives retail investors little protection if the working-capital bet goes wrong (S1, S2)

blocks.text: Bench Mark Infotech Services was incorporated in Kolkata on 9 January 2007 and converted to a public company on 22 June 2026 (S1). It describes itself as a 'single-window' IT and digital infrastructure system integrator. It designs, supplies, installs, commissions and maintains LAN/WAN networks, wireless systems, structured cabling, audio-visual and smart-classroom systems, CCTV/fire-alarm/boom-barrier security systems, outdoor racks and enclosures, and, since FY25, data-storage and data-centre setups (S1, S3). In practice it is a project integrator. It buys hardware from OEMs and authorised distributors against confirmed purchase orders, then installs it and bills against milestones. It does not manufacture anything (S1).

There are two smaller lines around the core projects business. First, AMC and facility-management contracts, which place technicians on-site or remotely to maintain installed IT infrastructure. Second, a fibre-optic vertical that leases dark fibre and bandwidth capacity to telecom operators and institutions under its DoT Infrastructure Provider Category-I (IP-I) registration, and also does trenching, ducting and restoration civil work (S1). The company has also announced new lines in AI labs (GPU computing, AI-ready infrastructure), camera/video analytics and cybersecurity (NGFW, UTM, endpoint, identity management). These are presented as strategy, and the revenue table shows no separate revenue from them yet (S1).

Operations run from a single rented registered office in Kolkata (lease to 31 Aug 2027) and a rented branch office in Patna, with technical staff deployed across eastern states (S1). Headcount is small: 45 employees at end-FY26, with a 31.46% attrition rate in FY26 (S1). A secondary source cites 54 employees as of 30 June 2026 (S4). The average project takes about 2-3 months to complete (S1). The company has been allotted leasehold industrial land by BIADA (Bihar). It has paid ₹1.49 cr as an advance, with ₹1.51 cr still committed, and is 'evaluating' a light assembly and testing facility there with no timeline set (S1).

Bottom line: this is an asset-light reseller-plus-installer of third-party IT hardware to government buyers in eastern India, with a modest recurring fibre-leasing income. The value added is in bid preparation, design, installation and execution, not in owned technology or manufacturing (S1).

subsections.title: How revenue is earned: segment, customer type and geography

blocks.caption: Service-wise revenue, ₹ lakh (% of revenue from operations) (S1)

blocks.text: The mix changes a lot from year to year, which is typical of a project business. The core networking line shrank from 60.91% of revenue in FY24 to 15.86% in FY26. Audio-visual jumped from ₹2.86 cr to ₹19.05 cr in FY25, and enclosures jumped from ₹0.64 cr to ₹8.85 cr in FY26 (S1). Only fibre leasing and AMC look recurring, together about ₹9.46 cr or roughly 15.6% of FY26 revenue (S1). By accounting line, 'IT infrastructure solutions projects' were ₹50.45 cr and 'sale of services' ₹10.08 cr in FY26 (S1).

Government and PSU work is won through tenders on GeM, state e-procurement portals and conventional bids. The company is also empanelled as a National Level System Integrator with BSNL and as a Business Partner with RailTel, which lets it reach central-government work through those PSUs (S1, S3). The RHP explains the jump in non-government revenue in FY26 as projects executed 'in collaboration with coal subsidiaries', mostly booked in Q3-Q4. That timing also explains why receivables ballooned at year-end (S1).

blocks.caption: Customer concentration, share of revenue from operations (S1)

blocks.text: The RHP does not name the top customers individually. Named clients across its disclosures include Airports Authority of India, BELTRON (Bihar State Electronics Development Corp.), RailTel, Indian Air Force, NTPC, Coal India subsidiaries (SECL, CCL, MCL) and Indian Railways (S3). The company also lists itself as a registered vendor to SAIL, IOCL, PGCIL, DVC, ONGC and CPWD (S1). Given that Bihar was 72.06% of FY25 revenue and the top customer 60.93%, the FY25 anchor client was very likely a Bihar state entity. That is an inference, not something the RHP states. The average relationship with the top customer is 11 years (S1).

blocks.caption: Supplier concentration, share of purchases + direct expenses (S1)

blocks.text: Materials are networking gear, fibre and LAN cable, racks, switches, routers and UPS units, bought per project with no long-term supply contracts (S1). The company says it is not dependent on a single OEM (S1). Supplier concentration is moderate and falling. The bigger issue is how much the company leans on supplier credit: payable days were 270 in FY26, and management plans to cut them to 183 days by FY28 using IPO money (S1).

The RHP's industry chapter is compiled from public sources (IMF, IBEF, NASSCOM, IMARC, SNS Insider) rather than a commissioned report. It is mostly macro and generic IT-services material, not a sizing of the government network-integration niche the company actually competes in (S1). The most relevant figures it cites: India's IT services market was US$39.83 bn in 2024. India's domestic IT and business services market was US$16.5 bn in 2024, growing 6.9% year on year. India's IT spending was projected at US$161.5 bn in 2025, up 11.1% (Gartner, as cited) (S1).

The RHP also cites a global network-as-a-service market of US$24.0 bn in 2024, projected by IMARC to reach US$185.0 bn by 2033 at a 25.5% CAGR (S1). That is a global, largely enterprise-cloud market and has little bearing on a Kolkata integrator installing CCTV and LAN for state agencies. The real demand drivers for BMISL are government digital-infrastructure budgets (smart classrooms, state networks, PSU campus networks, railway and coal-sector connectivity). The RHP does not size these (S1).

The industry section offers no addressable-market figure for government IT/network system integration in eastern India and no market-share estimate for the company. Growth claims rest on generic IT-sector tailwinds (S1).

The RHP names three listed peers as comparable: Dynacons Systems & Solutions, Xtranet Technologies and Esconet Technologies (S1). On scale alone (valuation is excluded from this report), FY26 total income was about ₹1,430 cr for Dynacons, ₹366 cr for Xtranet and ₹358 cr for Esconet, against ₹64 cr for BMISL (S1). The company is therefore a small player even among small-cap integrators.

blocks.caption: Scale versus RHP-named peers, FY26 total income (S1)

blocks.text: Beyond listed peers, the company itself says it competes with 'domestic and international IT service providers, infrastructure management companies, system integrators, cloud service providers and consulting firms', some with more money and bigger teams (S1). Government tenders are typically awarded to the lowest bidder once eligibility criteria are met (S1). BMISL won 14 of 46 bids in FY26, a 30.43% win rate, down from 37.25% in FY25 and 41.07% in FY24. The value of bids it won in FY26 was ₹10.40 cr against ₹67.69 cr bid (S1).

No genuine moat is visible. The strengths the RHP lists are an integrated model, long customer relationships, execution track record, OEM relationships and experienced promoters (S1). Every system integrator claims these. The RHP makes no import-substitution claim, no 'only/one of few' claim, and no proprietary technology or IP claim. Its main credentials are ISO 9001/27001, the IP-I registration, and BSNL/RailTel empanelment (S1, S3). Many competitors hold the same or can obtain them with modest effort.

items: Weak barrier: ISO 9001:2015 and ISO/IEC 27001:2022 certifications are commodity credentials (S1, S3)

Moderate barrier: the DoT IP-I registration (held since 2009) enables fibre leasing, which is the stickiest revenue line at 11.93% of FY26 revenue. But IP-I registration is widely held and the RHP flags it as a regulatory dependence (S1, S6)

Moderate barrier: 19 years of pre-qualification history (past project values, turnover thresholds) helps it qualify for mid-sized state tenders. Yet the falling win rate suggests this is not holding off competitors (S1)
No barrier: pricing. Tenders go to the lowest qualified bid and the company resells third-party hardware (S1)

blocks.text: Verdict on moat: none. BMISL is a regional, relationship-driven, lowest-bid integrator. Its margins depend on project mix and are not protected by any structural advantage (S1).

blocks.caption: Restated profit and loss, ₹ lakh (S1, S2)

blocks.text: On paper the trend is strong: revenue up 1.8x and PAT up almost 7x in two years (S1). Management attributes the FY26 margin jump to 'higher-margin projects', more AMC and fibre-maintenance work, and a deliberate move toward larger government contracts and away from small low-margin jobs (S1). Direct expenses nearly doubled (+89.44%) while traded-goods purchases fell 15.34%, which the company explains as a shift toward service-heavy integration work (S1).

Three things reduce confidence in the headline. First, FY26 other income of ₹3.46 cr was mostly ₹2.93 cr of old creditor balances written back as no longer payable. That is about 21.5% of pre-tax profit and is non-recurring (S1). Second, in the same year ₹1.11 cr of sundry asset balances was written off and ₹0.41 cr provided as bad debts, so the balance sheet is being cleaned up in both directions (S1). The company's own 'operating EBITDA' (excluding other income, adding back the write-off) is ₹11.70 cr, a 19.34% margin, still a large improvement on 15.04% in FY25 (S1). Third, the MD&A oddly states that the FY26 revenue increase was 'primarily attributable to the write-back of certain long-outstanding... vendor balances'. That looks like a drafting error, since write-backs sit in other income, but it is the kind of inconsistency that should not appear in an offer document (S1).

Restatement cut profits. Audited PAT was ₹11.73 cr in FY26 versus ₹10.22 cr restated, ₹6.02 cr in FY25 versus ₹5.83 cr, and ₹2.04 cr in FY24 versus ₹1.48 cr. Adjustments included prior-period items, unrecognised gratuity, unrecorded MSME interest, omitted insurance expense, depreciation errors and sundry balances written off (S1).

blocks.caption: Balance sheet and working-capital snapshot, ₹ lakh unless stated (S1, S2)

blocks.text: Formal debt is low, and the promoters also lend: ₹1.38 cr of unsecured promoter loans were outstanding at FY26, repayable on demand (S1). Bank working-capital lines from Punjab National Bank are priced at RLLR + 0.35% (8.45%) and personally guaranteed by both promoters (S1). The real financing of the business, however, is supplier credit. Payables at 270 days almost match receivables at 280 days. In other words, BMISL collects slowly from government customers and pays its vendors almost as slowly, and it has accrued ₹17.93 lakh of MSME penal interest for late payment (S1).

The ageing is the red flag. ₹10.17 cr of receivables, 18.50% of the book, is over one year old, including ₹1.46 cr over three years old, against a provision of just ₹0.41 cr (S1). Government counterparties rarely default outright, but they often dispute or delay final bills. The fact that the company is itself suing a BELTRON-project sub-contractor over invoices dating from 2014-17 shows how long such amounts can stay stuck (S1).

Over three years the company reported ₹17.53 cr of PAT but generated only ₹4.64 cr of operating cash, a conversion rate of roughly 26% (S1). FY25's positive operating cash flow came almost entirely from stretching payables by ₹15.80 cr. When payables stopped growing in FY26, operating cash flow went negative by ₹6.77 cr and year-end cash fell to ₹1.09 cr (S1). The RHP itself carries a risk factor titled 'We have experienced negative cash flows in the past three financial years' (S1).

The growth story does not yet pay for itself. Each rupee of new revenue ties up roughly 0.9 rupees in receivables, and the IPO is being raised to fund exactly that gap. Until operating cash flow tracks profit, reported PAT should be treated as provisional (S1).

sections.title: Issue details and objects of the issue

blocks.caption: Offer terms (S1, S2, S3)
rows: 38,58,000 shares; up to ₹42.44 cr at upper band
4,58,000 shares by promoter Vineet Kumar Gupta; ₹5.04 cr at upper band
QIB up to 18,30,000 (incl. 10,96,800 anchor); NII at least 5,50,800; individual investors at least 12,84,000

blocks.text: The task brief described the price band as not yet known. However, the band of ₹104-110 was published before the issue opened and is reported consistently by multiple sources (S2, S3, S5, S13, S14, S15). The RHP itself shows the price as '[●]', which is normal for an RHP (S1). About 11.9% of the issue by shares is an OFS, whose proceeds go to the promoter, not the company (S1, S2). The pre-IPO capital is almost entirely bonus shares. A 100:1 bonus in May 2026 took shares from 1,07,650 to 1,08,72,650, and a few shares were transferred at ₹100 in June 2026 to five individuals, including the CFO and a non-executive director (S1).

Of the ₹42.44 cr raised at the upper band, ₹5.04 cr goes to Vineet Kumar Gupta through the OFS, not to the company. After offer expenses, which the RHP has not yet quantified, the company keeps somewhat less than ₹37.40 cr (S1, S2).

subsections.title: Objects of the issue in full

blocks.caption: Use of net proceeds of the fresh issue, ₹ lakh (S1)
rows: [●]; capped at 15% of amount raised or ₹10 cr, whichever lower
[●]; shared pro rata with selling shareholder (listing fee borne by company)

blocks.text: The only named object is working capital. The RHP projects net working capital rising from ₹13.08 cr at FY26 to ₹30.22 cr at FY27 and ₹51.59 cr at FY28. That rise is driven by receivables growing from ₹54.98 cr to ₹70.96 cr and then ₹94.52 cr, and by a planned cut in payable days from 270 to 183 (S1). IPO money supplies ₹10 cr and ₹20 cr of that increase, with internal accruals and a ₹3 cr bank line making up the rest (S1). The cash conversion cycle is projected to lengthen from 14 days (FY26) to 103 days (FY28) (S1).

None of the objects has been appraised by a bank or independent agency. No monitoring agency is required because the issue is under ₹50 cr, so utilisation will be tracked only by the company's own audit committee (S1). One aggregator page showed object figures of ₹93.50 cr for working capital and ₹90 cr for debt repayment. These contradict the RHP and the ₹42.44 cr issue size and were disregarded.

What the money buys: time to collect from slow-paying government customers, and the ability to pay vendors faster. It creates no productive asset and no new capability. The BIADA land plan is funded separately and remains at a 'preliminary evaluation stage' (S1).

items: Minimum promoter contribution: up to 28,54,530 shares (20% of post-issue capital) locked in for 3 years from allotment (S1)
Promoter holding above the minimum contribution: 50% locked for 2 years and the remaining 50% for 1 year (S1)
Other pre-IPO shareholders (the five holders of 20 shares each): 1 year (S1)
Anchor investors: 50% for 90 days and 50% for 30 days from allotment (S1). A news report dates these lock-ins to 29 Dec 2026 and 30 Oct 2026 respectively (S7)

blocks.text: Pre-IPO equity is 99.99% held by the two promoters, so the practical overhang after listing comes from anchors (30- and 90-day lock-ins) and from promoter shares becoming free after 1 and 2 years (S1). None of the promoter shares are pledged (S1).

SME lock-ins here are shorter than a retail investor might assume. After 1 year, about 37.8 lakh shares become free to sell. That is half of the promoters' holding above the 20% minimum contribution, or roughly 36% of their post-issue stake (S1).

The company is controlled by a married couple. Vineet Kumar Gupta (48) is Chairman and MD, has been a director since incorporation in 2007, holds a B.E. in Electronics & Communication from Magadh University (2002), and claims over 20 years in IT and networking. He owns 69.81% pre-issue (S1, S11). Juli Gupta (41) is an Executive Director, has been on the board since December 2016, holds a B.A. from Dibrugarh University, has 9 years in designing IT infrastructure, NOCs and AV systems, and owns 30.19% (S1). Post-issue the promoters will hold 72.97% (S2, S5).

blocks.caption: Board and KMP (S1)
rows: FY26 pay ₹102 lakh; cap ₹120 lakh with up to 50% annual increments
FY26 pay ₹30 lakh; spouse of MD
Ex-Tanla Solutions, Apeejay Securities; holds 20 shares
Practising company secretary; director on 8 other companies

blocks.text: Every independent director, the audit committee (constituted 20 Jul 2026), the CFO and the CS were put in place within three months of the RHP. This is a board assembled for listing, not one with a governance track record (S1). The promoters' combined FY26 pay of ₹1.32 cr equals about 13% of restated PAT, and the approved ceiling allows the MD's pay to rise quickly (S1).

blocks.caption: Key related-party transactions, ₹ lakh (S1)
rows: Sales to Bizarre Infratech Pvt Ltd

blocks.text: Most RPTs are routine: promoter pay, promoter loans that support liquidity, and small reimbursements. Three features deserve attention. (1) Sales to promoter-group entities reached ₹2.57 cr (4.25% of revenue) in FY26 (S1). Bizarre Infratech, which bought ₹1.29 cr, reported revenue of only ₹45 lakh in FY25 and is authorised to do the same business as BMISL. So is Benchmark ISP Pvt Ltd. The company has signed non-compete agreements with both (S1). (2) 'Benchmark Infotech', a proprietorship of a relative with a near-identical name, received advances of ₹83.17 lakh in FY24 and has been a customer (S1). (3) The promoter's other venture, Leksa Lighting Technologies, reported FY25 revenue of ₹67.82 cr and PAT of ₹10.54 cr. That is larger than BMISL in the same year, which raises a fair question about where promoter time and attention go (S1).

The RPT picture is not egregious, but it is not clean either. The group has same-line entities kept apart only by non-compete agreements, sales to thinly capitalised affiliates, and a similarly named relative's firm. Watch whether affiliate sales grow after listing (S1).

items: Wrong financial statements were attached to AOC-4 filings for FY22 and FY23, and some omitted the RPT notes. A compounding application under Section 441 was filed on 31 Jul 2026 and is pending (S1)
Securities premium was not disclosed separately in the FY18-FY21 and FY24-FY25 financial statements. This is being reported to the ROC via GNL-2 (S1)
Charges for vehicle loans (Daimler Financial FY17, HDFC Bank FY19) were never registered with the ROC. The loans have since been repaid (S1)

MSME-1 returns were not filed for FY24-FY26 despite dues over 45 days. They were filed only before the RHP. ₹3.88 cr was disallowed under Section 43B(h), and ₹17.93 lakh of MSME penal interest has accrued (S1)
Past delays in TDS, ESIC and EPF filings led to penalties and interest, which the company attributes to portal glitches (S1)

Litigation is small: one arbitration filed by the company (₹65.54 lakh claim against Shani Peripherals over a 2014-17 BELTRON Wi-Fi project), and five tax matters totalling ₹19.34 lakh. There are no criminal, regulatory or civil cases against the company, the promoters or the directors (S1)

blocks.text: No single item is serious. Taken together, though, they describe a company whose finance and secretarial functions were informal until the IPO process began. That matters when the investment case depends on trusting reported receivables and profits (S1). The promoters are not wilful defaulters, are not debarred by SEBI, and have no litigation against them (S1).

items: Cash conversion and receivables: operating cash flow was negative in FY26 despite ₹10.22 cr PAT. Receivables are at 280 days, and ₹10.17 cr of them are over one year old. If collections slip further, profits turn into write-offs (S1)

Customer and geographic concentration: the top 10 customers are 94.19% of revenue and Bihar, Odisha and West Bengal are 80.04%. Losing one state programme or one PSU client can remove a quarter of revenue (S1)

Tender dependence with a falling win rate: 73.10% of revenue comes from government. Tenders are lowest-bid, and the win rate dropped from 41.07% to 30.43%. No long-term contracts exist with customers (S1)
Earnings quality: 21.5% of FY26 pre-tax profit came from creditor write-backs, and restatement reduced audited profits. Future margins may not match FY26 (S1)

Governance and compliance: there are multiple historical ROC, MSME and statutory-filing lapses, the board and KMP were constituted only in 2026, and the promoter-group entities work in the same line of business (S1)
Execution and people: a 45-person company with 31.46% attrition is attempting to add data-centre, AI-lab and cybersecurity lines, and it depends heavily on the MD's relationships (S1)

Bank guarantees: government tenders require EMDs (about 2%) and performance guarantees (about 10%) backed by bank lines and promoter personal guarantees. Faster growth needs more guarantee capacity (S1)

blocks.text: Many of the RHP's 20-plus risk factors are standard boilerplate, such as technology change, customer support and leased premises. The ones above were chosen because each has hard numbers behind it in the same document and each directly affects whether reported profit becomes shareholder cash (S1).
The key risk is the first one. The whole investment case, and the use of the IPO money, rests on government receivables eventually being collected in full (S1).

Lock-ins are shorter than on the mainboard. Only 20% of post-issue capital is locked for 3 years. Half the promoters' excess holding is freed after 1 year and the rest after 2 years. Anchor shares unlock after 30 and 90 days (S1). The minimum retail ticket is ₹2.64 lakh, and trading will be in 1,200-share lots on NSE Emerge with a single market maker, so exit liquidity may be thin (S2, S6).

Because the issue is under ₹50 cr, no monitoring agency will oversee use of proceeds. General corporate purposes and offer expenses were still '[●]' in the RHP (S1). Several aggregators also report inconsistent issue numbers, for example fresh-issue values of ₹35.27 cr versus ₹37.40 cr. Investors should rely on the final prospectus (S2, S9).
Regulatory: the fibre-leasing line, 11.93% of revenue, depends on keeping the DoT IP-I registration. Any cancellation or rule change would hit the only clearly recurring revenue stream (S1).

Management's only concrete forward statements are in the RHP. The strategy section lists: expanding service offerings (security, AV, data centre, power/electrical); expanding optical-fibre infrastructure 'across multiple geographies'; building out marketing and business-development teams; entering data storage and data-centre solutions (begun 'during the current year'); AI-lab and GPU-computing solutions; and cybersecurity (S1). None of these comes with revenue targets, order values, capex or timelines.

The most quantified forward-looking disclosure is the working-capital projection. It implies management expects receivables to reach ₹70.96 cr by FY27 and ₹94.52 cr by FY28 at about 280 days (S1). Mechanically, that implies revenue of roughly ₹90-120 cr by FY28, but this is an analyst inference from the WC model, not stated guidance. The BIADA land in Bihar is being evaluated for an assembly and testing facility with 'no definitive implementation timeline' (S1).

No order book figure was found in the RHP sections reviewed, and secondary coverage also reports none disclosed (S6). Press releases around the issue contain no management quotes on growth or plans (S10). There is no investor call or interview on record.

The history supports some continued growth, since government digital-infrastructure spending in eastern India is real and the company has 19 years of relationships (S1). But the FY26 data point in the wrong direction on visibility. The number of successful tenders fell from 23 to 14. The value of FY26 tender wins was only ₹10.40 cr. And FY26's growth leaned on non-government coal-sector projects booked late in the year that had not been collected by year-end (S1).

items: Positive: a rising recurring base (fibre leasing ₹7.22 cr, AMC ₹2.24 cr) and an entry into data-centre work, ₹3.87 cr in FY26 (S1)
Negative: no order book disclosure, a falling win rate, and new verticals (AI labs, cybersecurity) that are resale-heavy and fiercely competitive (S1)
Unknown: whether the FY26 margin level (19.34% operating EBITDA) survives a return to more traded-hardware-heavy projects (S1)

blocks.text: Treat the growth story as unproven until at least one post-listing half-year shows positive operating cash flow and stable receivable days.

blocks.text: These are day-1 figures only. The issue runs to 29 Sep, and SME QIB and HNI books typically fill on the last day, so nothing conclusive can be read from them yet (S7, S12). A third tracker showed a lower 0.21x total, reflecting a different update time (S8). The anchor book on 24 Sep placed 10,96,800 shares for ₹12.06 cr (S2, S7). The anchor investor names were not found in any source reviewed.

Grey market premium (unofficial, unregulated, and not an investment signal) was reported inconsistently: ₹16 on 25 Sep (S9), ₹12 (S5), and ₹0 on 25 Sep (S4). One tracker logged mostly ₹0 with two ₹12 readings on 21-22 Sep (S6). The spread itself suggests thin, unreliable grey-market activity.
Subscription and GMP play no part in the verdict. They are shown for completeness only.

method: Primary source: the Red Herring Prospectus (382 pages), downloaded from the IPO Watch-hosted copy and read page by page. Sections read directly: risk factors (pp. 26-39), RPT summary (pp. 59-61), capital structure and lock-in (pp. 75-87), objects of the offer and working-capital projections (pp. 88-95), basis-of-offer KPIs and peer list (pp. 98-100; peer P/E figures deliberately excluded), industry overview (pp. 110-123), business (pp. 127-151), management (pp. 172-178), promoters and group companies (pp. 186-193), restated cash flow and restatement reconciliation (F-7 to F-14), MD&A (pp. 209-213) and litigation (pp. 222-224). Restated figures were cross-checked against Chittorgarh, Outlook Business, IPO Watch and Multibagg, and they match. The DRHP was not read separately: the RHP supersedes it, and the DRHP link on the company site was not opened. The S1 date is the access date; the RHP's own filing date was not captured, though its restated financials carry an auditor sign-off dated 29 Jul 2026. The task brief said the price band was not yet known, but ₹104-110 was published before opening and is reported by several sources, so it is used here. No valuation metric is included. Gaps: anchor investor names were not found; subscription data is day 1 only (issue closes 29 Sep 2026); no order book figure was found; no management interview or call exists. One aggregator's object figures (₹93.50 cr working capital, ₹90 cr debt repayment) contradict the RHP and were disregarded. Some derived numbers are the analyst's own arithmetic on RHP figures: cumulative operating cash flow vs PAT, write-back as a share of PBT, peer scale multiples, and the implied FY28 revenue range. S13-S15 were seen only as search results and are used solely to corroborate the issue dates, venue and terms. GMP figures are unofficial and conflict across trackers.
